title: The polygraph doesn't test lies, it tests the fear that makes you confess
dek: US courts rejected the polygraph's science, yet allowed police to use it to extract confessions—its value was never detecting lies, but manufacturing confessions and ongoing surveillance through psychological fear.
why: Traces the polygraph from its invention through legal restrictions, explaining where workplace and job-screening polygraph requirements came from.
who: Job candidates required to take polygraph tests during interviews or hiring, and those concerned with workplace surveillance and interrogation ethics.
skip: Skip NPR ad breaks at the beginning and middle (around 0:00, 4:13).

points.h: First case solved, suspect may never have been guilty
points.body: The 1921 Berkeley theft case where police used a polygraph on a female suspect, who panicked and fled, then confessed after days of continued surveillance. The inventor Larson later doubted her guilt—she had psychological issues and the thefts continued afterward. This "first solved case" suggests the polygraph's value wasn't finding the truth, but extracting confession through humiliation and pressure.

points.h: The polygraph was invented to monitor police, not criminals
points.body: Created in 1920s Berkeley by August Vollmer (the "father of modern policing") and physiologist John Larson to civilize brutal police practices. The first people systematically polygraphed were Berkeley police themselves—the tool was used for internal accountability to prove police weren't breaking the law, building public trust in the technology before use on suspects.

points.h: Courts banned polygraph evidence while police kept using it in interrogation rooms
points.body: In United States v. Frye, a murder suspect confessed then recanted; the polygraph showed innocence but the judge barred the jury from hearing it. The case established the Frye rule: only evidence vetted by the scientific community is admissible in court. But police continued using polygraphs to pressure suspects in interrogation rooms—police are legally permitted to lie and use deception to elicit statements that can later be introduced in court, regardless of the polygraph's scientific validity.

points.h: The polygraph became a tool for continuous employee surveillance in corporate America
points.body: Leonard Keeler, a colleague of Larson's, brought the polygraph to Chicago in the 1930s and sold testing services to banks and retailers like Walgreens. Found that employees often confessed to small thefts during tests. When management wanted to fire them, Keeler advised against it: knowing they could be polygraphed anytime made these employees the most honest. The tool transformed from a crime-solving instrument into a system of continuous workplace surveillance, spreading through banking, retail, and federal agencies.

points.h: Large-scale polygraph screening creates impossible statistical problems
points.body: When used at Los Alamos and Oak Ridge on thousands of nuclear weapons project employees, Ken Alder points out that even if the polygraph worked perfectly (it doesn't), mass screening produces enormous false positives—all the innocent people get investigated while actual liars slip through. The tool might have some value for a single suspect, but applied to an entire workforce, the mathematics breaks down entirely.

points.h: A Secretary of State threatened resignation to ban workplace polygraphs
points.body: From the 1960s onward, unions and the public opposed polygraph abuse; by the 1980s about half the states had banned it in employment. But it remained legal federally. When Reagan wanted to use polygraphs to hunt leakers in government, Secretary of State George Shultz declared it scientifically worthless and threatened to resign. This prompted Congress and Reagan to sign the Employee Polygraph Protection Act in 1988, banning private-sector employee testing, though government security, police, and pharmaceuticals were exempted. Industry scale collapsed from its peak.

points.h: The polygraph masks subjectivity with the false objectivity of technology
points.body: Ken Alder frames this as a very American story, like the SAT—seemingly machine-scored, objective, and fair, yet SAT is criticized for hidden bias. The polygraph is the same: who determines if someone is lying isn't the machine but the operator's subjective reading of the waveforms. The belief that "a neutral machine can solve social problems" is itself a distinctly American myth.

points.h: The polygraph may create nothing more than security theater
points.body: Alder concludes the problem isn't just that polygraphs don't detect lies, but that they create "security theater"—like airport metal detectors, giving false reassurance while not actually improving safety. He closes with Montaigne's 450-year-old observation: truth has one face, but liars have a thousand; extracting truth from someone's mind is a game that's hard to win.
